title: Delhi's Smog Blind Spot: Farm Fires Now Lit After NASA's Satellites Pass Overhead
excerpt: Stubble burning in Punjab has shifted to 4-6 p.m., after India's monitoring satellites pass at midday, so official fire counts miss most large fires and overstate the decline, NASA and iFOREST analyses show.
body:
• NASA analysis shows most Punjab stubble fires are now lit between 4 p.m. and 6 p.m., after India's main fire-monitoring satellites have passed overhead.
  • iFOREST's 2025 analysis found over 90% of large farm fires in Punjab now occur after 3 p.m., up from about 3% in 2021.
  • Measured by burnt area rather than fire counts, burning in Punjab and Haryana is down only about 25-35% from peak years, iFOREST estimates.
  • Evening fires are worse for Delhi: weaker night winds let smoke accumulate near the ground, and NASA's Pawan Gupta estimates crop fires can supply 40-70% of the capital's pollution on peak days.

Delhi's smog has a timing problem. New analyses by NASA scientists and the Delhi-based think tank iFOREST show that farmers in Punjab and Haryana have shifted stubble burning to the late afternoon and evening, hours after the polar-orbiting satellites India uses for official monitoring have passed. The fires still burn, and the smoke still reaches the capital. The count, however, misses most of them.

A blind spot built into the orbit

India's primary monitoring relies on the MODIS and VIIRS instruments, whose satellites pass over northern India between about 10:30 a.m. and 1:30 p.m. and record only fires actively burning at that moment. Hiren Jethva, an atmospheric scientist at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center who has tracked stubble burning for nearly a decade, used high-frequency data from South Korea's GEO-KOMPSAT-2A geostationary satellite, which images the region every 10 minutes, to check what the polar orbiters miss. His finding: where burning once peaked between 1 p.m. and 2 p.m., most fires are now detected between 4 p.m. and 6 p.m. "Farmers have changed their behavior," Jethva said.

"Our analysis provides incontrovertible evidence that India's current stubble-burning monitoring system is structurally misaligned with ground realities."

— Chandra Bhushan, CEO, iFOREST

iFOREST's 2025 status report puts a number on the shift: over 90% of large farm fires in Punjab now occur after 3 p.m., compared with about 3% in 2021. A 2025 study in Current Science, using European Meteosat data, found the same drift, with peak fire activity moving from about 1:30 p.m. in 2020 to about 5 p.m. in 2024.

What the recount does to the progress story

Official claims of success rest on fire counts, and by that measure the fall looks dramatic, with the government citing a decline of roughly 90% in burning incidents in 2025 compared with 2022. Measured by burnt area across the full day, iFOREST's multi-satellite analysis tells a flatter story: a reduction of about 25-35% in Punjab and Haryana since the peak years, credited to crop-residue machinery and other alternatives. The gap between those two numbers is the story. A monitoring system can record success while the underlying activity declines far more slowly.

Why evening smoke hurts Delhi more

The shift is not only an accounting issue. Fires lit at dusk burn into hours when winds weaken and a temperature inversion traps pollutants near the ground, so the same field can produce worse exposure than it would at midday. NASA research scientist Pawan Gupta estimates stubble burning can account for 40-70% of Delhi's pollution on individual peak days, falling to roughly 20-30% averaged across the season, though estimates of the fires' share vary widely by study.

The official response so far

The Centre has already adjusted on paper. At an October 14 review, Union Environment Minister Bhupendra Yadav directed Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan to run ground monitoring and flying-squad patrols specifically after 3 p.m., naming hotspot districts including Sangrur, Tarn Taran, Amritsar, Karnal and Kurukshetra, and ordered farm-fire data linked with the Central Pollution Control Board and the Commission for Air Quality Management. The scientists' prescription goes further: combine polar and geostationary satellite data, and judge the season by burnt area, not by a fire count taken at lunchtime.
